The Angel Island chuckwalla (Sauromalus hispidus) is a large, robust iguanid lizard endemic to Isla Ángel de la Guarda in the Gulf of California. Resting metabolic rate measurements obtained through closed-system respirometry at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] yielded a maximal oxygen consumption of 0.8418 milliliters per minute [JOi = 0.8418 milliliters per minute]. This value, recorded from adults during their active seasonal period, aligns closely with predictions based on body size for other large-bodied Sauromalus species and reflects the relatively low standard metabolic rate typical of herbivorous lizards that inhabit arid, resource-limited environments. The measurement was taken during daylight hours when individuals exhibit peak voluntary activity, ensuring that the recorded oxygen consumption represents a true basal condition rather than a postprandial or stressed metabolic state. This species is among the largest members of its genus.

Females of this species attain sexual maturity after a prolonged juvenile phase. Data collected from a field population monitored at a mean ambient temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] indicate that the interval between hatching and the onset of gonadal activation spans approximately 2.5 years after hatching [tp = approximately 2.5 years after hatching]. This extended pre-reproductive period is unusual even among iguanids and likely reflects the slow growth trajectory imposed by the limited primary productivity of the desert island habitat. Unlike many smaller lizards that mature within a single season, Sauromalus hispidus appears to channel resources into structural growth and fat storage for several years before allocating energy toward reproductive structures. The timing of maturation is inferred from repeated captures of marked individuals, with the first observation of vitellogenic follicles or enlarged testes used as the criterion for puberty.

The reproductive output of this species is characterized by a moderate clutch size and an extended laying interval. Females deposit a single clutch of 8 eggs [N_R_i = single clutch of 8 eggs] during each breeding season, and they are capable of producing one clutch annually [F_R_i = one clutch annually] when maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This reproductive strategy, with a low annual egg production relative to body mass, is consistent with the life history of other long-lived, slowly maturing herbivorous lizards. The constraints on clutch frequency are likely mediated by the energetic demands of vitellogenesis in a female that must also maintain large lipid reserves to survive the prolonged dry season. The single annual reproductive event contrasts sharply with the multiple clutches produced each year by smaller, more fecund iguanid congeners. The maximum reproduction rate is therefore estimated at 8 eggs per year [Ri = 8 eggs per year] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C].

Eggs deposited in the nest chamber and incubated at a constant temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C] require approximately 90 days [ab = approximately 90 days] to complete embryonic development and achieve hatching. This protracted incubation period is not unusual for large eggs with substantial yolk reserves, which must be metabolized slowly to sustain the developing embryo over the entire thermal regime. At the moment of shell pipping and subsequent emergence, the hatchlings weigh approximately 7.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 7.5 grams]. This neonatal mass is low compared to the adult body weight but is sufficient to support the young through the first weeks of independent foraging. The emergence of hatchlings coincides with the late summer monsoon season, when ephemeral vegetation provides the necessary nutrition for rapid early growth. The age at birth is a critical life-history parameter influencing juvenile survival.

Maximum recorded longevity in the wild, based on recapture data from a long-term mark-recapture study conducted at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], is estimated at approximately 60 years [am = approximately 60 years]. This extraordinary lifespan places Sauromalus hispidus among the longest-lived lizards known, exceeded only by certain tortoises and tuataras. The resting oxygen uptake of 0.8418 milliliters per minute [JOi = 0.8418 milliliters per minute] measured at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] aligns with this extreme lifespan, as a low rate of cellular metabolism is generally correlated with reduced oxidative damage and delayed senescence. The ultimate adult wet weight of 1400 grams [Wwi = 1400 grams] is attained gradually over many decades, reflecting the slow but indeterminate growth pattern common among large-bodied iguanid lizards that continue to add skeletal mass throughout life. Individuals continue to grow slowly throughout life, and the largest territorial males can exceed this asymptotic mass, though females typically remain smaller. The combination of extreme longevity, low metabolic expenditure, and delayed reproduction represents a classic bet-hedging strategy in a stochastic desert environment.
